consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on a settled core: the Flood (paradigmatically Noah's flood, Genesis 6-9) symbolizes divine judgment on human sin paired with the salvation of a righteous remnant, with two NT-fixed extensions—baptismal typology (1 Peter 3:20-21) and eschatological warning of sudden final judgment (Matthew 24:37-39; 2 Peter 3). Secondary readings include de-creation/re-creation, covenant sign, and (in Responses A and B) flood imagery as overwhelming trouble or invading enemies.
book_summary: The book identifies the flood as 'an army in motion'—either an invading nation or the Lord's own host sweeping the enemy away—citing prophetic texts (Isaiah 8:7; Jeremiah 47:2; Daniel 9:26) where flood/overflowing-waters imagery explicitly denotes military invasion, and cross-referencing a Sea & Waters chapter.
consensus_core_identification: Flood = God's judgment on universal wickedness together with preservation of a faithful remnant, typologically extended to baptism and to the final eschatological judgment (grounded in the Noah narrative).
book_core_identification: Flood = an army in motion; a symbol of military invasion (a nation invading, or God's own host as the invader).
boundary_disagreement: The consensus centers on the Noahic flood narrative and its judgment/salvation/baptism typology; the book's entry does not treat Noah's flood at all, instead defining 'flood' via prophetic invasion oracles. Cases central to the consensus (Genesis 6-9, 1 Peter 3, Matthew 24) are absent from the book's entry, while the book's cases (Isa 8:7; Jer 47:2; Dan 9:26) appear in the consensus only as a secondary alternative ('invasion of enemies' in Response B; 'overwhelming trouble/persecuting opposition' in Response A).
material_contradiction: As the primary identification of the symbol, 'flood = an army/military invasion' cannot coexist with 'flood = divine judgment-and-salvation typology anchored in Noah's flood and baptism.' Accepting the book's identification as the symbol's meaning replaces the consensus's central referent (the Noah narrative and its NT typology) with a different referent (prophetic invasion imagery). The army could function as an instrument of judgment, giving some conceptual overlap, but the identifications are not equivalent and the book gives no common-view note acknowledging the consensus reading.
rationale: The book's core identification substitutes a different central referent: rather than the Noahic judgment-salvation-baptism complex that every blind response treats as the settled primary meaning, the book defines flood as invading armies drawn from prophetic texts. This is not mere narrowing of the consensus category (judgment) because the book specifies a concrete, different symbolic decode (army in motion) and grounds it in a different textual corpus. It is not NOVEL because Responses A and B both list enemy-invasion/overwhelming-opposition flood imagery as a recognized alternative (citing Isa 59:19, Dan 9:26, Rev 12:15-16). Elevating a listed secondary alternative to the exclusive primary, while omitting the consensus core, constitutes replacement of the central identification: DIVERGENT.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED rather than DIVERGENT: the book's 'army as flood' can be read as a specification of the broader consensus category of divine judgment (Isa 8:7 explicitly has the LORD bringing the Assyrian 'waters'), and enemy-invasion flood imagery already appears as a common alternative in the blind responses, so the book arguably narrows within an acknowledged strand rather than contradicting the tradition outright.
